As I write this, a GreaseMonkey script (thanks @frankenmine) is deleting all my comments at Reddit. The TamperMonkey program didn't work with Chrome, so I dug out Firefox for this one. I haven't coded/edited in a while, and this was a very simple method.

If you've done this before, you know the feeling. All those great jokes, inspiring top-level comments, recycled memes, and well-researched responses are gone, forever, never to be seen by the public eye again. In fact, the only people who will ever see that content again will be a shadow agency or the judicial system, and that's only if they demand your IP records from Reddit, Inc. You'd basically have to commit an act of terrorism for that to happen.

If you haven't been through this before, it's like burning your old phone(s) with texts on them, old college essays, and personal notes passed in high school. It takes a measure of resolve, even though the content you're destroying is almost entirely useless and inconsequential to anyone but yourself. Besides, the content is yours, and humans are natural hoarders.

For me, it came down to principles, and mine are set diametric to those of Reddit. For me, destroying my history with Reddit was a deliberate gesture. Reddit heard squeaky wheels, and instead of replacing or ignoring them, they greased them, and installed more squeaky wheels, knowing the cacophony was music to the ears of squeaky critics. Out of principle, and a little spite, today I chose to completely disassociate myself.

..but I'm getting ahead of myself..

I joined Reddit very late, in Feb 2015. I was going through a life-altering personal tragedy, and needed a new distraction after deleting Facebook for a second time. I had heard about Reddit in 2010 from a buddy, so I decided to start an account. The layout took some getting-used-to, karma climb was exciting.

I was thrilled at the freedom of expression there. The idea was simple: Message boards for anything you can think of, but since it was user-driven and managed, there would be no official policy outlawing....words. This was unlike anything I'd experienced before, since I'd had well-reasoned comments censored at places like NPR, west coast dailies, and even blogs starved for reader activity. This was always frustrating, since those comments never included lewd or abusive language, and I knew the deletions were politically motivated.

Alas, within 17 days I was shadowbanned. I recounted the experience on my blog. The short story is that I was shadowbanned for posting original, scientific content on the 2016 Presidential race to Reddit at two different subs (in which I was active) in too short a time frame. I asked admins for an explanation. No answer. I started a new account with the same handle I have here on Voat, with my middle finger sticking straight up.

By the Spring of 2015, I'd started hearing about shadowbans being used more frequently, allegedly to silence users whose views didn't align with those of mods and admins in San Francisco. Hell, it happened in an AMA with Julian Assange, as if the irony weren't thick enough already.

Then the purges started. I ate a lot of popcorn through the first one, and supported the blackout. By the time the second purge came in July, I had split. Yishan's warning prior to the executive transition was enough for me. In August, Huffman banned "abusive and offensive speech," officially sanctioning the safe spaces that had begun to form under Pao. July is when Voat traffic spiked, and that's why you see a lot of subverses and users here with the most recent activity dated 5 months ago. I'm one of the guys who stuck around.

Voat was fresh air after living in the smog of political correctness and double-standardization over at Reddit. Sure, I had to block a bunch of rude, violent, and otherwise NSFW subs when I got here. Even today, I have to restrain myself from responding to every ill-mannered bigot, and I have to remember that a lot of internet users are just looking for a fight.

Still, it's a relief to know that whatever I post will be seen by people who don't agree with me. My voice has been heard, and I'm forced to hear other voices. For example, I'm a Christian, ethnically anyway, and I learn a lot from hearing all the atheists here talk about why they hate (or simply don't believe in) God.

In fact, their criticism is what reinforces my beliefs, and this is the fundamental difference between Voaters and Redditors.

We can handle criticism. Redditors can't.

We're open to all ideas. Redditors aren't.

We represent reality. Reddit doesn't.

In 2015, Reddit chose a side. This was very calculated, and from a financial perspective, a practical decision. However, as I stated above, I'm a man of principle, as we should all be (women of principle, transgendered people of principle, attack helicopters of principle, etc). The greatest companies and civilizations in history have had principles, and lacking or compromising them has been disastrous.

One could say that Reddit established their principles by banning subs and silencing users, but I would direct anyone believing that to the suicide of Reddit's co-founder, Aaron Swartz, in 2013, and the Forbes interview of another co-founder, Alexis Ohanian, in 2012 saying that he wanted Reddit to be a "bastion of free speech."

Swartz died for his principles of open-source content and freedom of information, Ohanian is still taking bids on his. Reddit's principles weren't established in 2015, they were modified for profit.

In 2016, be a person of principle. Even if I don't agree with your principles, I'll respect you for having them.
